The answer above follows a pattern common in Welsh: a leading consonant cluster followed by a high-frequency vowel. How to read common Welsh digraphs without overforcing them

Welsh has several two-letter combinations that count as single sounds. DD represents an unvoiced th (like in "think"), while LL approximates a voiceless L with aspiration. These don't appear in English Wordle strategies, so most solvers have no muscle memory for them.

The clue widget on today's page highlighted a position containing DD. If you flagged that square yellow but didn't know what sound to expect next, you weren't alone. The trick is treating each digraph as one unit during elimination, not two separate letters competing for space.

For tomorrow's board, build a short list of common Welsh openings: CH, DD, FF, NG, LL, RH, TH. When one appears in the reveal card, lock that position mentally and work outward. Don't let your brain try to split it into English equivalents.

Where English guessing habits break the solve

The biggest trap on Worgle boards is assuming Q, X, and Z are rare. In Welsh, those letters barely appear. Instead, W and Y function as vowels much of the time. A word like CWYTH contains no traditional vowel, yet it's perfectly valid.

Players conditioned by English Wordle often waste a guess testing words heavy with Q or Z, expecting those tiles to show up eventually. On Welsh boards, that guess is usually dead money. The archive section shows previous weeks rarely featured either letter before position four.

Today's solution contained a Y in the middle. If you held back on Y-heavy guesses because English taught you Y is supplementary, that's the gap to close. Welsh treats Y as a core vowel—sometimes sounding like a short I, sometimes like a schwa. Respect that role when building candidate lists.

How to handle tomorrow's Worgle more smoothly

Before guessing tomorrow, spend thirty seconds on Welsh letter frequency, not word lists. W appears in roughly one of every four valid answers. Y isn't far behind. Meanwhile, J, Q, and Z combine for less than three percent of entries.

Use the solver tool to input your known greens and yellows, then filter for Welsh-compatible candidates. The standard Wordle dictionary will steer you wrong here—it doesn't account for Welsh orthography at all.

Questions players keep asking

Is Worgle harder than regular Wordle?

Difficulty depends on your background, not the puzzle itself. Native Welsh speakers often find English Wordle harder. For English-dominant players, Welsh letter distribution creates genuine friction—that's the learning curve, not a flaw in the puzzle.

Why does Welsh have so many double letters?

Double letters in Welsh often mark historical sound changes or indicate the start of a new syllable. LL and DD aren't decorative—they represent distinct phonemes. Treat them as atomic units and your solve rate improves noticeably.

Can players use the same opening words from English Wordle?

Some overlap exists, but Welsh-optimized openers perform better. Words like TRAOD (troubles) and LLAIS (voice) score high on positional entropy for Welsh boards. The solver can generate custom openers if you prefer not to build your own list.

The game validates against the Welsh word list only. An English-plausible spelling that isn't on the Welsh list returns as invalid—you'll see the red border just like any bad guess. Double-check the archive if you're unsure whether a candidate exists in the Welsh dictionary.

No. Answers display in plain ASCII Welsh spelling. Accented characters appear in some written Welsh but the puzzle strips them for consistency. Focus on the base letters and let the hint widgets guide stress positions.

worldle-answer-today.articleHtml:
Today's Worldle puzzle shows a country silhouette that rewards players who think in continental chunks rather than isolated geography trivia. The reveal card and hint widgets on this page confirm the pattern: continent recognition gets you close, then the directional arrow and distance percentage do the heavy lifting.

Worldle answer today: what the silhouette should suggest first

The first thing to check against the silhouette isn't coastline detail—it's bulk shape and position relative to recognizable neighbors. A rough outline that spans multiple time zones usually signals a large country; compact shapes tucked between mountain ranges point toward smaller nations with distinct borders. The archive link on this page lets you compare today's silhouette against previous reveals if you're second-guessing regional fit.

A careful player notices that Worldle's silhouettes preserve coastline indentations more faithfully than interior mountain ranges. That deep bay on the eastern edge? That's not noise—that's geographic signal. Cross-reference it against the direction arrow before guessing a country that shares only a similar outline but sits in the wrong hemisphere.

How direction and distance clues narrow the shape

The directional arrow tells you roughly where your guess lands relative to the target—not just cardinal direction, but angular relationship. If your guess appears northeast of the target country, expect the real answer to sit southwest along that same latitudinal band. Combined with the distance percentage, which scales based on real-world kilometers, you can triangulate position within a handful of candidate nations.

The percentage hint deserves more attention than most players give it. A 45% match doesn't mean "half right"—it means your guessed country sits roughly 55% of the maximum possible distance away from the target across Earth's surface. That math favors large countries when distances run high, and penalizes island nations heavily even when they're geographically close. Check the solver tool on this page to test guesses against those two variables simultaneously.

Why neighboring countries become the easy wrong answer

After a few correct guesses, players learn to cycle through immediate neighbors first. It's efficient, but it creates a trap: neighboring countries often share similar silhouettes and comparable distance percentages, making them hard to distinguish without additional context. The directional arrow alone can't separate France from Spain if both sit adjacent to your guess and return similar readings.

The fix is to anchor on a known landmark—a distinctive peninsula, major river delta, or capital city position visible on the silhouette—before cycling through neighbors. Today's puzzle likely includes at least one such anchor if you've already made two or three attempts. Look for the feature that breaks symmetry: the outlier notch, the elongated extension, the sudden narrowing that no adjacent country shares.

How to finish tomorrow's Worldle with fewer detours

Build your opening guesses around geographic extremes rather than obvious choices. A massive country from one continent and a small island nation from another give you two extreme data points in opposite directions, dramatically shrinking the search space. If both extremes return low similarity scores, the target country probably sits somewhere in the middle—neither huge nor tiny, neither polar nor equatorial.

Keep notes on which distance percentages correlate with which country sizes in your region. Over weeks, you'll develop intuition for what a "high 30s" versus "low 50s" percentage implies for specific continents. The archive accessible through this page tracks your historical patterns if you want to review past solves without relying on memory alone.

Questions players keep asking

Does the distance percentage account for projection distortion?

Worldle uses great-circle distance calculated on Earth's actual spherical surface, not flat map projections. That means northern hemisphere countries closer to the poles will show slightly different percentage behavior than equatorial nations of equivalent real-world distance. Factor this in when comparing polar countries against tropical ones.

Can the directional arrow ever point backward from the guess?

Yes—the arrow always points from your guessed country toward the target. If you're guessing north of the answer, the arrow points south. Players sometimes misinterpret this as the arrow showing "which direction to move," when it's actually showing where the answer lies relative to their current guess.

Why did two countries with identical silhouettes score differently?

Silhouette matching accounts for shape, but the distance and direction hints add a positional layer. Two countries might look nearly identical from a shape perspective—one could sit 800km away while the other sits 3,200km away. The percentage difference reflects that real-world gap, not shape quality.

Should I always start with the largest country on each continent?

It's a reasonable strategy for eliminating broad regions quickly, but smaller countries with unusual shapes—Indonesia's archipelagic sprawl, Chile's extreme elongation, Norway's fractured fjords—often provide better contrast on subsequent guesses. Mix size extremes with shape extremes for faster elimination.
